answer.rationale: The two live deficits are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly addresses both. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 is exactly the cautionary case: it bought top-line signups (+31%) and revenue (+18%) while early retention fell 12pp, which is the opposite of sustainable qualified revenue; it also held acquisition channels fixed, so it does not even describe our current competitive situation. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are healthy but do not target the observed regression. I spend verification on the two memories that are load-bearing for my chosen action rather than on the ones I am already declining. memory_86 is the direct basis for the action and I need to know whether 'improved completion and time-to-value' was ever measured through to retention and qualified revenue, or whether it only measured the funnel metric it optimized — the memory_73 pattern warns that a completion lift can be a measurement artifact of asking less of the user. memory_31 matters because 'cutting required fields' has a specific downstream hazard: fewer qualifying fields degrades the routing signal that feeds the demo-request path memory_44 says outperforms self-serve for enterprise, so an SMB activation win could quietly tax enterprise pipeline quality. I also note memory_86 (day 52) and memory_31 (day 12) may describe overlapping or even the same underlying result consolidated twice, which would mean I have less independent evidence than the memory list implies. Because these downstream effects are unverified, I run a small guarded test with a holdout, instrumented on week-four retention, enterprise demo-request rate, and qualified revenue — not completion rate alone. If verification shows memory_86 measured only completion, I hold the conclusion loosely and let the guardrails, not the inherited summary, decide whether to scale.
